message.content:
The total number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large – on the order of **10⁴³**.  

This figure, often called the *Shannon number*, was first estimated by Claude Shannon in 1950. It represents an upper bound on the number of possible arrangements of pieces on the board that satisfy all the rules of chess (including pawn promotion, castling rights, and en‑ passant possibilities).  

For comparison, the number of possible complete games (i.e., sequences of moves from start to finish) is even larger, roughly **10¹²⁰**. Both numbers are far beyond the total number of atoms in the observable universe, illustrating why exhaustive search of the entire game tree is impossible.
